## What the Britannica entry (COINAGE, E0100) says about how coins were made

The entry defines coinage as "the art of making money, as performed either by the hammer or mill." It describes two processes:

**The older hammer method:** A large metal plate was cut into small squares, the corners trimmed with shears, and each piece shaped and gently hammered into a round blank called a "planchet." Engravers prepared a pair of steel dies ("mauls"); one die was fixed into a block like a vise, the planchet was laid on it, and the movable die was struck "with several heavy blows, with a hammer of an enormous size, till the double stamp was sufficiently, in relief, impressed on each side of the planchet." Inspectors then judged the weight, fineness, and mark to make it "good current money." {E0100, scan page britannica:309f765b1ecc83e0a7f7762e44b4a927a7555443:train:1250}

**The improved mill method:** Cast metal plates ("laminae") were passed between rollers of a "laminating engine" to give uniform thickness (instead of beating on an anvil). A steel "trepan" cut planchets directly from the lamina. The planchets were weighed, filed, boiled and cleaned, then passed through an edge-marking machine and finally "the mill," which "squeez[ed] each of them finely between the two dyes, ... with one blow," forcing the metal to fill the engraved figures. A separate machine stamped legends or rings onto the coin edges. {E0100, same scan page}
